questions.stem:
Soil A has pH 5.0 and soil B has pH 6.0.
How does the H+ activity in soil A compare with soil B?

options.misconception: It compares the pH numbers directly, as if 6/5 meant something.
It treats one pH unit as a doubling.
That's the difference for two pH units, not one.

questions.explanation: pH is the negative log (base 10) of H+ activity, so each unit is a factor of 10. A soil at pH 5 has ten times the H+ activity of one at pH 6.

questions.stem: In an acid clay soil, where is most of the acidity?

options.text: Held on clay and organic matter surfaces as reserve (exchangeable and residual) acidity
Dissolved in the soil water, where the pH meter measures it
options.misconception: The pH reading only sees the small active fraction in solution.

options.text: In the rainwater that fell on it
options.misconception: Rain starts acidification, but the acidity ends up stored in the soil.
Roots release some H+, but they don't store the soil's acidity.

questions.explanation: Reserve acidity on colloids can be thousands of times larger than the active acidity in solution. That's why pH alone can't tell you how much lime a soil needs.

questions.stem: Why are strongly acid soils (below about pH 5) toxic to many crops?

options.text: H+ ions burn the roots directly
options.misconception: H+ matters, but the main damage comes from what the acidity dissolves.

options.text: Aluminium dissolves as Al3+, which damages root tips

options.misconception: Acidity slows some N processes but doesn't remove all the nitrogen.
Acid soils are usually short of calcium, not overloaded with it.

questions.explanation: Below roughly pH 5.5, aluminium from clay minerals and oxides dissolves as toxic Al3+, which stunts root growth. Liming precipitates it back out as Al(OH)3.

questions.stem: The same soil is measured in water and in 0.01 M CaCl2. How does the CaCl2 reading usually compare?

options.text: Higher, because calcium is a base
options.misconception: Ca2+ isn't a base. It doesn't remove H+.
The salt changes what's in the solution.

options.text: It can't be measured, because soil pH needs pure water
options.misconception: 0.01 M CaCl2 is a standard method.

options.text: Lower, because Ca2+ swaps exchangeable H+ and Al3+ into solution

questions.explanation: Calcium displaces some reserve acidity into solution, so the CaCl2 pH is usually about 0.5 units lower. It's also more stable, because it evens out seasonal differences in soil salt.

questions.stem: What is cation exchange capacity (CEC)?

options.text: The amount of positive charge on soil surfaces
options.misconception: Soil colloids are mostly negative. That's why they hold cations.

options.text: The total amount of exchangeable cations a soil can hold on its negative charges
The concentration of cations dissolved in soil water
options.misconception: That's the soil solution, not the exchange sites.

options.text: How much nitrate the soil can store
options.misconception: Nitrate is an anion.

questions.explanation: Negatively charged clay and humus hold cations like Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and NH4+ that can swap with the soil solution. CEC is reported in cmol(+)/kg.

questions.stem: Which soil would have the highest CEC?

options.text: A sandy soil with little organic matter
options.misconception: Sand has very little charged surface.
All clays feel similar, but kaolinite has a low CEC.

options.text: A smectite clay soil rich in organic matter

options.misconception: Quartz carries almost no charge.

questions.explanation: Smectite (about 80 to 120 cmol(+)/kg) and humus (often 200 or more) both carry lots of negative charge. Kaolinite is only about 3 to 15, and quartz is near zero.

questions.stem: A soil holds 2 cmol of Ca2+ per kg on its exchange sites. How much CEC does that occupy?

options.misconception: It forgets that each Ca2+ carries two charges.
It divides by the charge instead of multiplying.

options.text: It depends on the soil pH
options.misconception: The conversion is fixed. Only the total CEC can vary with pH.

questions.explanation: CEC counts charge, so multiply moles by the ion's charge: 2 × 2 = 4 cmol(+)/kg. Numerically, cmol(+)/kg is the same as the older meq/100 g.

questions.stem: Adding compost raises CEC much more in a near-neutral soil than in a very acid one. Why?

options.text: Humus has permanent charge from isomorphous substitution
options.misconception: That's how clay minerals get charge, not humus.
Acidity slows decomposition rather than speeding it up.
Humus charge depends strongly on pH.

options.text: Humus charge comes from carboxyl and phenolic groups that lose H+ as pH rises

questions.explanation: Organic matter's charge is pH-dependent. At low pH its acidic groups keep their H+, so little negative charge is available. Near neutral, more groups ionise and the CEC climbs.

questions.stem: Where does most of smectite's permanent negative charge come from?

options.text: Broken edges of the clay crystals
options.misconception: Edges matter most for kaolinite, and their charge varies with pH.
Nitrate is negative but isn't part of the clay.
Rain doesn't build charge into the crystal.

options.text: Isomorphous substitution, such as Mg2+ replacing Al3+ in the crystal

questions.explanation: When a lower-charge ion takes the place of a higher-charge one as the mineral forms, the layer is left with a net negative charge that doesn't depend on pH. That's permanent charge.

questions.stem: Why does smectite swell when wet while kaolinite barely does?

options.text: Smectite layers are loosely held, so water and cations get in between them; kaolinite layers are hydrogen-bonded tightly

options.misconception: Kaolinite has far less charge than smectite.
Smectite particles are typically smaller.
Kaolinite is a classic clay mineral.

questions.explanation: Kaolinite's 1:1 layers are hydrogen-bonded to each other, so water can't get in. Smectite's 2:1 layers are held loosely by hydrated cations, so the interlayer expands. That's why smectite soils crack wide in summer.

questions.stem: Illite is a 2:1 clay like smectite, but it swells very little. Why?

options.misconception: Illite has a high layer charge.

options.text: K+ ions fit snugly between the layers and lock them together

options.misconception: Illite is 2:1.
Illite is crystalline.

questions.explanation: Potassium fits into the hexagonal holes of the tetrahedral sheets and isn't easily hydrated, so it pins the layers shut. That also fixes K, which plants can only get at slowly.

questions.stem: Highly weathered tropical soils (like Oxisols) are dominated by kaolinite and Fe/Al oxides. What does that mean for their CEC?

options.text: Very high, because old soils accumulate nutrients
options.misconception: Weathering strips out high-charge minerals and nutrients.

options.text: Only positive charge at every pH
options.misconception: Oxides can be positive in acid conditions, but their charge varies with pH.

options.text: Low, and much of it depends on pH
The same as a young soil
options.misconception: Mineralogy changes a lot as soils weather.

questions.explanation: Kaolinite and oxides carry little permanent charge, so CEC is low and comes mainly from pH-dependent surfaces and organic matter. Keeping organic matter is critical in these soils.

questions.stem: Per kilogram, which usually has the highest CEC?

options.misconception: Smectite is high, but humus is usually higher.
Kaolinite is one of the lowest-CEC clays.
Quartz is close to zero.

questions.explanation: Humus can reach 200 to 400 cmol(+)/kg, more than smectite at about 80 to 120. A few percent of organic matter can supply much of a soil's CEC.

questions.stem: Straw with a C:N ratio of about 80:1 is dug into soil. What happens to plant-available nitrogen in the short term?

options.text: It rises quickly as the straw releases N
options.misconception: Straw has too little N for the microbes eating it.
Decomposers interact strongly with soil N.

options.text: It turns into nitrate and leaches immediately
options.misconception: The straw ties N up rather than releasing it.

options.text: It falls, because microbes take up soil N to break down the straw

questions.explanation: Decomposers need food at roughly 24:1 C:N. High-carbon residues force them to pull mineral N from the soil (immobilisation), so crops can go short until decomposition catches up.

questions.stem: How does organic matter improve soil structure?

options.text: It's heavy, so it packs particles together
options.misconception: Organic matter is light. It loosens soil.

options.text: It makes the soil totally water-repellent
options.misconception: Some dried organic matter repels water, but that's a problem, not the structure benefit.

options.text: Organic glues and cation bridges bind mineral particles into stable aggregates

options.misconception: Organic matter binds clay rather than dissolving it.

questions.explanation: Microbial gums, fungal hyphae and humus bridged by Ca2+ hold particles together as aggregates. That leaves pores between them for air and water.

questions.stem: A soil test reports 2% organic carbon. Roughly how much organic matter is that?

options.misconception: Organic matter also contains O, H, N and other elements.
It multiplies by 0.58 instead of dividing.
It mistakes the carbon fraction for the answer.

questions.explanation: Organic matter is roughly 58% carbon, so organic matter ≈ organic carbon × 1.72, which is about 3.4% here. The factor is a rough average, and some labs use 2.

questions.stem: What is base saturation?

options.text: The share of CEC held by H+ and Al3+
options.misconception: That's acid saturation, the opposite.

options.text: The percentage of the soil that is limestone
options.misconception: It mixes up base saturation with carbonate content.

options.text: The share of CEC held by Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+
The pH at which the soil's CEC is full
options.misconception: Base saturation is a percentage of CEC, not a pH.

questions.explanation: These 'base' cations don't hydrolyse to make acidity. High base saturation usually goes with a higher pH.

questions.stem: Which cation is held most strongly on soil exchange sites?

options.misconception: Sodium is common but held weakly.
A single charge is held less strongly than higher charges.
Ca2+ is held strongly, but a triple charge beats it.

questions.explanation: Higher charge and a smaller hydrated size mean stronger holding, roughly Al3+ > Ca2+ > Mg2+ > K+ ≈ NH4+ > Na+. That's why Na+ leaches easily once it's displaced.

questions.stem:
A soil has a CEC of 20 cmol(+)/kg, and its exchangeable Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+ add up to 15 cmol(+)/kg.
What is its base saturation?

options.misconception: That's the acid saturation.
It divides the CEC by the bases.
It reads the bases total as a percentage.

questions.explanation: Base saturation = bases ÷ CEC × 100 = 15 ÷ 20 × 100 = 75%. The other 25% is held by acidic cations.

questions.stem: A farmer applies a lot of ammonium (NH4+) fertiliser. What happens on the exchange sites?

options.text: Nothing, because the sites are already full
options.misconception: Exchange is dynamic. Full sites still swap.

options.text: NH4+ swaps onto the sites by mass action, pushing other cations into solution where they can leach
NH4+ attaches only to positive sites
options.misconception: Cations are held on negative sites.
CEC is a property of the surfaces, not of what's on them.

questions.explanation: Exchange is reversible and driven by concentration. Flooding the solution with NH4+ displaces Ca2+, Mg2+ and K+, which can then be lost in drainage water.

questions.stem: What defines a sodic soil?

options.text: A high exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP above about 15)
High electrical conductivity from any salts
options.misconception: That's a saline soil.
That's a calcareous soil.
Sodic soils are usually alkaline.

questions.explanation: Sodicity is about sodium on the exchange sites; salinity is about total dissolved salt. A soil can be saline, sodic, both or neither.

questions.stem: Why do sodic soils have such poor structure?

options.text: Sodium cements particles together too tightly
options.misconception: It does the opposite. It pushes particles apart.

options.text: Na+ has a single charge and a large hydrated size, so clay particles disperse and clog pores
Sodium kills the microbes, so structure collapses
options.misconception: The main effect is physical dispersion, not biology.
Sodic soils tend to be alkaline.

questions.explanation: A single, bulky hydrated charge can't hold clay plates together, so the clay disperses. The surface seals, water can't soak in, and the soil sets hard when it dries.

questions.stem: Why is gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) used to fix sodic soils?

options.misconception: Gypsum is nearly neutral. Raising pH is lime's job.

options.text: Sulfate locks the sodium in place
options.misconception: The goal is to remove sodium, not lock it in.
Gypsum is a mineral salt.

options.text: Its Ca2+ replaces exchangeable Na+, which is then leached away

questions.explanation: Gypsum is soluble enough to supply Ca2+, which out-competes Na+ for exchange sites and flocculates the clay. Water then has to drain through to carry the sodium away.

questions.stem: What does the electrical conductivity (EC) of a soil extract measure?

options.misconception: Every dissolved ion carries current, not just Na+.
pH is measured separately.

options.text: Total dissolved salts (all the ions in solution)

options.misconception: Organic matter isn't measured by conductivity.

questions.explanation: More dissolved ions carry more current, so EC (in dS/m) is a quick measure of salinity. Above about 4 dS/m in a saturated paste extract, a soil is classed as saline.

questions.stem: Why does nitrate leach more easily than ammonium?

options.misconception: Size isn't the issue. Charge is.

options.text: Nitrate is an anion, so negatively charged colloids don't hold it, while NH4+ is held on the CEC

options.misconception: Ammonia (NH3) can be lost as gas. Ammonium stays dissolved or held.
Sand holds almost nothing.

questions.explanation: Most soils carry far more negative than positive charge, so cations like NH4+ are held while NO3- moves freely with draining water.

questions.stem: What does nitrification (NH4+ → NO3-) do to soil pH?

options.misconception: It gets the direction backwards.
The reaction releases acid.

options.text: Lowers it, because the reaction releases H+
Only affects pH in waterlogged soils
options.misconception: Nitrification needs oxygen, so it happens in aerated soils.

questions.explanation: Converting one NH4+ to NO3- releases two H+. Long-term use of ammonium fertilisers is a major cause of soil acidification.

questions.stem: Where is denitrification (NO3- → N2O and N2) most likely?

options.text: In waterlogged, low-oxygen soil with plenty of available carbon

options.misconception: Denitrifiers only use nitrate once oxygen runs out.
Cold slows it down.
Lime isn't required.

questions.explanation: When O2 is scarce, bacteria use nitrate as their electron acceptor and release N2O and N2. That's lost nitrogen, and N2O is a potent greenhouse gas.

questions.stem: Urea is spread on the surface of a moist, alkaline soil and not worked in. What's the main risk?

options.text: It instantly becomes nitrate and leaches
options.misconception: Urea goes through ammonium first, and that takes time.
Urea is uncharged and isn't held by clay.

options.text: It's lost straight away by denitrification
options.misconception: Denitrification needs nitrate and low oxygen.

options.text: It hydrolyses to ammonium and some escapes as ammonia gas

questions.explanation: Urease converts urea to ammonium carbonate, raising the local pH so NH4+ turns into volatile NH3. Working the urea in or watering it in cuts the loss.

questions.stem: At roughly what soil pH is phosphorus most available to plants?

options.text: pH 4, because acid dissolves phosphate minerals
options.misconception: Acid soils lock P up with iron and aluminium.
In alkaline soils, calcium phosphates form.
P availability is very pH-sensitive.

questions.explanation: Below about 5.5, iron and aluminium bind phosphate. Above about 7.5, calcium does. The window of best availability sits in between.

questions.stem: In strongly acid soils, what mainly fixes phosphate?

options.misconception: Calcium is the main fixer in alkaline soils.
Nitrate doesn't react with phosphate.
Sodium phosphates are soluble.

questions.explanation: Phosphate adsorbs strongly onto Fe and Al oxide surfaces and precipitates as Fe and Al phosphates. Liming towards neutral releases some of it.

questions.stem: Why does phosphate rarely leach, unlike nitrate?

options.text: Phosphate is a cation held on the CEC
options.misconception: Phosphate is an anion.
Phosphate has no common gaseous form in soils.

options.text: Phosphate binds strongly to minerals and precipitates with Fe, Al and Ca
Plants take all of it up immediately
options.misconception: Most applied P stays in the soil, not the plant.

questions.explanation: Phosphate forms strong bonds directly with oxide surfaces (specific adsorption), so it stays close to where it was applied. Most P losses come from erosion instead.

questions.stem: How does most farm phosphorus reach rivers and lakes?

options.text: By leaching through deep soil, like nitrate
options.misconception: P is held too strongly to move like nitrate.

options.text: By erosion and runoff carrying P attached to soil particles

options.misconception: P has no common gaseous form in soils.
That's a nitrogen process.

questions.explanation: Because P sticks to soil, it travels with eroded sediment and surface runoff. Keeping soil in place is the main way to protect waterways from algal blooms.

questions.stem: A soil becomes waterlogged. Once the O2 is used up, which is reduced next?

options.misconception: Rotten-egg smells are memorable, but sulfate is reduced much later.
Iron comes after nitrate and manganese.
Making methane from CO2 is the very last step.

questions.explanation: Microbes use electron acceptors in order of energy yield: O2, then NO3-, Mn(IV), Fe(III), SO4 2- and finally CO2.

questions.stem: Why are waterlogged subsoil horizons often grey or blue-grey?

options.misconception: Fe3+ gives red, orange and yellow colours.
Salt crusts are white and form at the surface.

options.text: Iron is reduced to soluble Fe2+ and moved away, leaving grey colours

options.misconception: Organic matter darkens soil brown or black, not blue-grey.

questions.explanation: This is gleying. Reduced iron is mobile and gets stripped out, exposing the grey of the underlying minerals. Rusty mottles mark where it oxidised again.

questions.stem: A flooded rice paddy smells of rotten eggs. What's producing the smell?

options.text: Sulfate being reduced to hydrogen sulfide (H2S)

options.misconception: That gives N2 and N2O, which are odourless.
Methane is odourless.
Ammonia smells sharp, not eggy.

questions.explanation: Under strongly reducing conditions, bacteria use sulfate as an electron acceptor and release H2S. It can also be toxic to rice roots.

questions.stem: What usually happens to the pH of an acid soil after it has been flooded for a few weeks?

options.misconception: It gets the direction backwards.
Flooding sets off reactions that use up acid.

options.text: It becomes strongly alkaline, around pH 10
options.misconception: It overshoots. pH settles near neutral.

options.text: It rises towards neutral, because reduction reactions consume H+

questions.explanation: Reducing Fe(III) and Mn(IV) uses up H+, so acid soils rise towards about pH 6.5 to 7 when flooded. Alkaline soils drift down towards neutral too, as CO2 builds up.

questions.stem: Two soils are both at pH 5.0: a sandy soil low in organic matter, and a clay soil high in organic matter. Which needs more lime to reach pH 6.5?

options.misconception: It holds very little reserve acidity.

options.text: The same amount, since the pH is the same
options.misconception: pH only shows active acidity.

options.text: The clay soil high in organic matter

options.misconception: Both are well below 6.5.

questions.explanation: Clay and humus hold far more reserve acidity, so they buffer harder against pH change. Lime requirement depends on buffer capacity, not on pH alone.

questions.stem: How does agricultural lime (CaCO3) reduce soil acidity?

options.text: Carbonate reacts with H+ to make CO2 and water, while Ca2+ replaces exchangeable acidity

options.misconception: Ca2+ is a spectator. The carbonate does the neutralising.
Lime doesn't work by changing moisture.
Lime is a mineral.

questions.explanation: CO3 2- + 2H+ → CO2 + H2O removes acidity. Ca2+ takes the place of exchangeable Al3+ and H+, which are then neutralised in turn.

questions.stem: Why does soil pH resist change when acid or base is added?

options.text: Soil has no ions to react
options.misconception: Soil is full of exchangeable ions.
Rain tends to acidify soil over time.

options.text: Microbes hold the pH exactly fixed
options.misconception: Microbes affect pH but don't hold it fixed.

options.text: Reserve acidity on colloids resupplies H+ to the solution as it's neutralised

questions.explanation: Exchange sites and pH-dependent surfaces act as a reservoir. Neutralise the solution and more H+ and Al3+ come off the colloids, so pH moves slowly.

questions.stem: A soil is over-limed to pH 8. Which problem becomes more likely?

options.misconception: Al toxicity is an acid-soil problem.

options.text: Deficiencies of iron, manganese and zinc

options.misconception: High pH can actually increase N loss as ammonia.

options.text: None, because more lime is always better
options.misconception: There's an optimum range.

questions.explanation: At high pH, Fe, Mn and Zn form insoluble oxides and hydroxides, and phosphate binds to calcium. Most crops do best between about pH 6 and 7.

questions.stem: Goethite (an iron oxide) has a point of zero charge around pH 8. At soil pH 5, what is its surface charge?

options.text: Positive, so it can hold anions like sulfate and phosphate

options.misconception: Many oxides are positive below their point of zero charge.
It's only neutral at about pH 8.

options.text: It's charged only when salt is added
options.misconception: Its charge comes from H+ gained or lost, which depends on pH.

questions.explanation: Below its point of zero charge, a surface picks up extra H+ and becomes positive. That's how acid, oxide-rich soils hold anions.

questions.stem: Where does variable (pH-dependent) charge come from?

options.misconception: That makes permanent charge.
CO2 affects solution pH but isn't a surface charge.
Salts change the soil solution, not where surface charge comes from.

options.text: Surface OH and COOH groups gaining or losing H+

questions.explanation: Oxide surfaces, clay edges and humus carry groups that gain H+ in acid conditions and lose it in alkaline ones, so their charge shifts with pH.

questions.stem: The pH of a variable-charge soil is raised from 5 to 6.5. What happens to its CEC?

options.misconception: It gets the direction backwards.

options.text: It stays the same, because CEC is fixed
options.misconception: Only the permanent-charge part is fixed.
Raising pH adds negative charge.

questions.explanation: At higher pH, more surface groups lose H+ and become negative, so the soil can hold more cations. Liming highly weathered soils raises their CEC this way.

questions.stem: Where is anion exchange capacity (AEC) most important?

options.text: In young soils rich in smectite
options.misconception: Smectite carries mainly negative charge.
At high pH, surfaces are mostly negative.

options.text: In highly weathered, acid soils rich in iron and aluminium oxides

options.misconception: Sand has little charge of any sign.

questions.explanation: Oxides below their point of zero charge carry positive charge, so acid tropical soils can hold some nitrate, sulfate and chloride. Most temperate soils have little AEC.

questions.stem: Why is clay so much more chemically active than sand?

options.text: Clay is made of more reactive elements
options.misconception: Both are mostly Si, Al and O.
Clay holds water, but that's not why it's chemically active.

options.text: Sand grains have no surface atoms
options.misconception: They do, just far fewer per gram.

options.text: Its tiny particles have a huge surface area per gram, and that surface is charged

questions.explanation: Clay particles smaller than 2 µm can have tens to hundreds of m² of surface per gram (smectite up to about 800), against well under 1 m²/g for sand. Soil chemistry happens at surfaces.

questions.stem: In the USDA system, what is the upper size limit for clay particles?

options.misconception: That's the upper limit for sand.
That's the sand–silt boundary.
That falls inside the sand range.

questions.explanation: Sand is 2 to 0.05 mm, silt is 0.05 to 0.002 mm, and clay is anything smaller than 0.002 mm.

questions.stem: Roughly what CEC does a pure quartz sand have?

options.text: Very high, because sand is everywhere
options.misconception: Being common doesn't make it reactive.
Quartz has far less charged surface.
Humus has one of the highest CECs of all.

questions.explanation: Quartz has a small surface area and almost no permanent charge, so it holds very few cations. Sandy soils rely on organic matter for their CEC.

questions.stem: A clay soil holds more total water than a sand. Why isn't all of it available to plants?

options.text: Much of it is held so tightly in tiny pores and on surfaces that roots can't pull it out

options.misconception: Salinity isn't the general reason.
Clay actually loses water slowly.
Plenty of crops grow well in clay.

questions.explanation: Plants can only use water held between field capacity and wilting point. Clays hold a lot of water below the wilting point, so loams often have the most available water.
